title: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns
goal: By the end you can say what `inline` does to the bytecode, use a non-local return on purpose, add `noinline` or `crossinline` when the compiler asks and know why it asks, and decide when a function should not be inline at all.
opening:
Picture a small print shop. Behind the counter sits a binder of procedure sheets: how to time a job, what to do when a printer jams. When a clerk takes a job, she can pass it to a colleague who knows the sheet, with a slip for the one step only she can do. Or she can photocopy the sheet into the job's own folder and do every step herself. The copy is quicker. It costs paper, though, and it never hears about corrections to the master.

Kotlin gives your functions the same choice, and `inline` is the photocopy. The surprise is that it changes what your code means, not only how fast it runs: a `return` inside a copied step can leave the whole job. Java habits walk straight into that.

The last track ended with Project Valhalla, which lets the JVM drop an object's identity. This track starts by dropping a whole object, the one behind a lambda. We'll watch the compiler make the copy, follow a `return` that leaves more than you expect, meet two modifiers for lambdas that can't be copied, and count the cost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

options: `null`, because `return` only leaves the lambda and `forEach` carries on
`"JAMMED job_2"`, because `return` leaves `firstJammed`
It doesn't compile: `return` is not allowed inside a lambda
It throws, because `forEach` can't be stopped early
warmup.why: `forEach` is an inline function, so its lambda is pasted into `firstJammed`, and a bare `return` there returns from `firstJammed` itself. That's a non-local return, and the section on it takes it line by line. In Java, `return` inside a `forEach` lambda would only leave the lambda, which is why the first option is tempting. Inside a lambda passed to an ordinary function, the third option would be right.

sections.h: When not to inline: code size, frozen copies and visibility
sections.body:
`inline` has three costs, and all three show up in real code.

The first is size. The body is copied into every caller, so a 40-line function called from 200 places becomes 200 copies, and every folder in the shop gets thicker. The compiler even warns when you inline a function that takes no lambdas: `expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. Inlining works best for functions with parameters of function types.` Without a lambda there is nothing to remove: no object, no call through an interface. And the JIT, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while the program runs, already inlines small, hot methods by itself.

The second is frozen copies. A caller gets its copy of the body when the caller is compiled. In one test, a small app was compiled against version 1 of a library. Then version 2 replaced the library's jar (the zip file a library ships in) without recompiling the app. The app printed `inline=v1 plain=v2`. The ordinary function ran the new code, and the inline one still ran its old copy. It's the photocopy that never heard about the correction.

So if you publish a library that other programs use, treat a public inline body like a public signature. A fix inside it reaches each program only when that program is rebuilt.

The third is visibility, and it follows from the second. The body lands in other **modules**, the separately compiled parts of a program, such as a library and the app that uses it. So it may only use what those modules can use. Call a private function from a public inline one, and you get `public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function.`

The fix is `@PublishedApi internal`. `internal` means visible only inside this module, and `@PublishedApi` makes the function public in the bytecode anyway, so the pasted copies can reach it. The helper's own body isn't copied anywhere, so it can use private state freely. Here it hands out trace ids, labels that tie the start and end lines of one operation together in the log:

```java
// Java has no internal or inline. The nearest shape: one public helper that callers reach
public final class Tracing {
    private static final AtomicInteger COUNTER = new AtomicInteger();
    public static String nextTraceId() { return "trace-" + COUNTER.incrementAndGet(); }
}
```

```kotlin
inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T {
    val id = nextTraceId()                  // must be reachable from every caller's module
    println("[$id] start $operation")
    val result = block()
    println("[$id] end $operation")
    return result
}

@PublishedApi
internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet()

private val counter = AtomicInteger()       // fine: nextTraceId is not inline
```

The compiler adds two hard limits. An inline function can't call itself (`inline function 'fun recI(n: Int): Int' cannot be recursive.`), and it can't contain a local function (`local functions are not yet supported in inline functions.`).

Properties can be inline too, as long as the accessor has no backing field, that is, no stored value of its own. The demo's `val Long.asKilos: String inline get() = ...` turns 1,999 grams into `1.999 kg`. You'll mostly see inline properties when they need a `reified` type parameter.

My rule: inline small functions that take lambdas, or that need `reified` or a non-local return, and leave everything else ordinary. When an inline body starts to grow, split it.

**Keep the inline part to a few lines, and move the real work into a @PublishedApi internal function that is compiled once.**

The lab puts all of this into one small helper: a retry for a printer that sometimes jams, with a non-local return, a `crossinline` lambda and a `@PublishedApi` door.

aside.title: Doesn't the JIT inline everything anyway?
aside.body: It inlines a lot, but it's a different tool. The JIT inlines while the program runs, only on hot paths, and it can undo its choice when its guesses turn out wrong. Kotlin inlines at compile time, at every call site, before the JVM ever sees the code. Only the compile-time kind can change what the code means, which is why a non-local `return` and a `reified` type need it. The lesson "Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics" in the performance track covers the JIT's side.

compare.title: Wrapping a callback API: Java Supplier vs Kotlin inline with crossinline

java.title: Timing.java

kotlin.title: Timing.kt

compare.note: Both versions time a step on another thread and hand back a future, a placeholder for a result that arrives later. In Java the caller's lambda is always an object, and `timedAsync` wraps it in a second one for `supplyAsync`. In Kotlin the compiler pastes both `timed` and the caller's lambda into one `Supplier` class that it generates for that call site, so there is one object instead of two, and no call through `Supplier.get` on the caller's code. The bigger difference is the rule for the caller: inside the Kotlin block, a bare `return` is a compile error, while a Java lambda simply can't express one. Java code that calls the Kotlin `timedAsync` gets the ordinary compiled body and passes a `Function0`.

worked.title: Write an inline helper over a Java callback API

steps.say: A Java library (invented for this example) lets one job at a time use the shop's printer. You pass the work as a `Callable`, the JDK's interface for a task that returns a value, and the library runs it while it holds the printer, so two jobs never mix their pages. You want Kotlin callers to write `queue.printing { printer.print(job) }`. Start with the API and an ordinary Kotlin wrapper.
The wrapper is one line and runs for every job, so make it inline. The compiler refuses, because `block()` is now called inside the `Callable`, which the library may run later or on another thread.

Add `crossinline`. The caller's lambda is now pasted into a `Callable` class that the compiler generates for each call site. In exchange, callers lose the non-local `return`: that's the rule `crossinline` enforces.

Check that it earns its place. It does: one line, a lambda parameter, called for every job. If it later grows logging, timing and error handling, keep the inline part to this one line and move the rest into a `@PublishedApi internal` function, so 300 call sites don't each carry a copy.

lab.title: An inline retry helper, sync and async
steps: A printer that jams on the first try often works on the second, so the shop's app retries. Run the tests. All eight fail with `NotImplementedError`. Read `Callers.kt` but don't edit it: the tests go through it, and its comment says why.
Write `retry` (TODO 1). Start at attempt 1, `return block(attempt)` inside a `try`, catch `Exception`, and decide whether to go round again. Keep the earlier failures in a list.
When you stop, `throw giveUp(attempt, e, earlier)`. The build now fails. Read the error, and fix the declaration of `giveUp` (TODO 2), not `retry`.
Write `retryAsync` (TODO 3) as `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ retry(maxAttempts) { block(it) } }, executor)`. Add the modifier the compiler asks for.
Run the tests until all eight pass, including `RetryFromJavaTest`, which calls your `retry` from Java with no inlining at all.
Optional: add `crossinline` to `retry`'s `block` and run again. `Callers.firstAccepted` stops compiling, because its `return printer` is a non-local return. Undo it.
hints: `require(maxAttempts >= 1) { "maxAttempts must be at least 1" }` throws `IllegalArgumentException` before the loop starts, so the block is never called.
A `while (true)` loop whose body ends only with `return` or `throw` needs no `return` after it. The compiler knows the loop never falls through.
The fix for TODO 2 is two words on the declaration: `@PublishedApi internal fun giveUp(...)`. `internal` keeps it out of the Kotlin API, and `@PublishedApi` lets public inline bodies call it.
`supplyAsync` stores a thrown exception in the future, and `get()` reports it as an `ExecutionException` whose cause is your `RetryExhaustedException`. You don't have to write anything for that.
lab.done_when: All eight tests in `RetryTest` and `RetryFromJavaTest` pass.

drill.title: Write timed and timedAsync from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an inline `timed(label, block)` that returns the block's result and prints the elapsed time even when the block throws. Then write `timedAsync(label, executor, block)` that runs `timed` on an executor and returns a `CompletableFuture`. Which parameter needs a modifier, and which one?

alt.title: Timing.java

recap: `inline` copies the function body and the bodies of its lambda arguments into each caller: no `Function` object, no call through an interface, no boxing of a generic result.

A bare `return` in a lambda passed to an inline function is a non-local return and leaves the enclosing function. `return@forEach` leaves only the lambda. Since Kotlin 2.2, `break` and `continue` work there too.

`noinline` keeps one lambda as a real object you can store or pass on. `crossinline` lets you call a lambda from another execution context (a `Runnable`, a `Supplier`, an object) by forbidding non-local returns in it.
Inline only small functions that take lambdas. Every caller carries a copy, and a public inline body stays frozen in a caller until that caller is recompiled.
A public inline function may only use public API. Reach a helper through `@PublishedApi internal`.
The limit: inlining helps only a lambda that runs right there, in the caller. Java never inlines Kotlin code; it calls the compiled body and passes `Function0` or `Function1` objects.
closing:
We started in a print shop that photocopies a procedure into each job's folder instead of handing it over with a slip. `inline` is that copy: no lambda object, no call through an interface, and a `return` that ends the whole job. `noinline` keeps a slip for the notice board, `crossinline` seals the night-shift envelope, and every copy stays frozen until its caller is rebuilt.

Now search your Kotlin code for a bare `return` inside `forEach {`. Each one leaves the whole function, not just the item.

Next, we'll let the compiler erase a different object: the wrapper class that gives a number its own type. When does a value class stay a plain `long`, and when does the box come back?

options: Nothing: it compiles as written
`cannot inline 'task' here: it might contain non-local returns`, and it suggests `crossinline`
`illegal usage of inline parameter`, and it suggests `noinline`
Inline functions can't call Java APIs such as `Executor`
quiz.why: `task` is called inside the `Runnable` lambda, which is another execution context. The compiler asks for `crossinline`, which forbids a `return` in the caller's lambda and still inlines its body into the generated `Runnable`. `noinline` would also make it compile, but the compiler suggests that one when you store or pass the lambda itself, and it gives up inlining the body.

options: `12 done`
`1 done`
quiz.why: `forEach` is inline, so the bare `return` leaves `process` the first time it sees 0. Nothing after that runs, not even `print(" done")`. `12 done` is what the Java habit expects, where `return` only skips one element; that would be `return@forEach` in Kotlin.

quiz.q: `shop-app` 2.0 was compiled against the library `print-tools` 1.4.0, and calls its public `inline fun <T> withRetry(block: () -> T)`. You upgrade `print-tools` to 1.4.1, which fixes a bug inside `withRetry`, and keep the `shop-app` 2.0 you already built. Which `withRetry` code runs when `shop-app` calls it?
options: The fixed 1.4.1 code, because the newest jar is on the classpath
Neither: the JVM throws `NoSuchMethodError`
The old 1.4.0 code, copied into `shop-app`'s bytecode when it was compiled
Whichever version the class loader happens to load first
quiz.why: An inline body is copied into the caller at the caller's compile time. `shop-app` never calls the `withRetry` method in the jar; it runs its own pasted copy of the 1.4.0 body. The classpath only decides which method exists, and nobody in `shop-app` calls it. Only rebuilding `shop-app` against 1.4.1 picks up the fix.

quiz.q: Which declaration makes the compiler warn `expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant`?
options: `inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T`
`inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T`
`inline fun <T> List<T>.sumPagesBy(selector: (T) -> Int): Int`
`inline fun toSheets(pages: Int): Int = (pages + 1) / 2`
quiz.why: `toSheets` has no function-typed parameter and no reified type parameter, so there is nothing for inlining to remove. The JIT would inline a hot small method like that by itself. `isA` has no lambda, but it needs `inline` for its reified `T`, so the compiler doesn't warn.

quiz.q: From the generics track: why does `inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA() = this is T` need `inline`?
options: Because reflection is slow, and inlining makes it fast
Because the reified type is stored in a hidden field of the lambda object
Because the JVM erases `T`, and only a copy of the body at each call site knows the real class
It doesn't: since Kotlin 2.0 `reified` works on ordinary functions too
quiz.why: Type arguments are erased at run time, so an ordinary function can't know what `T` was. An inline function's body is compiled again at each call site, where the type argument is written in plain sight, and the compiler can put a real `instanceof` there. Ordinary functions still can't have reified type parameters.

flashcards.front: What does `inline` do to a function and the lambdas passed to it?
flashcards.back: The compiler copies the function body and each lambda body into the call site. No `Function` object is created and nothing is called through an interface.

flashcards.front: Inside `fun f()`, what does the `return` in `list.forEach { if (it == 0) return }` leave?
flashcards.back: The whole function `f`. It's a non-local return, allowed because `forEach` is inline. `return@forEach` would leave only that lambda call.

flashcards.front: When does the compiler ask for `noinline`?
flashcards.back: When you use an inline lambda parameter as a value: store it in a field, add it to a collection, or pass it to a non-inline function.

flashcards.front: When does the compiler ask for `crossinline`?
flashcards.back: When you call the lambda from another execution context, such as an object, a `Runnable` or another lambda. `crossinline` forbids non-local returns in the caller's lambda.

flashcards.front: Why is a public inline function's body part of your library's binary interface?
flashcards.back: Callers get a copy of the body when they are compiled. Change the body, and an old caller keeps running its old copy until it is recompiled.

flashcards.front: A public inline function calls a `private` helper. What happens, and what is the fix?
flashcards.back: Compile error: `public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function.` Mark the helper `@PublishedApi internal`.

flashcards.front: What does Java see when it calls a Kotlin inline function?
flashcards.back: An ordinary static method that takes `Function0`/`Function1` objects. javac inlines nothing. A reified inline function is synthetic, so javac can't see it at all.

terms.plain: A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site, together with the bodies of the lambdas passed to it.
A place in the code that calls a function. With inline, this is where the copy of the body ends up.
A lambda that uses variables from outside its braces. Unless it is inlined, the JVM keeps those values in a small object.
A bare `return` inside an inlined lambda. It leaves the function that contains the lambda, not just the lambda.
`return@forEach`: leaves only the current call of the lambda, like `continue` in a loop.
Marks one lambda parameter of an inline function as an ordinary object, so you can store it or pass it on.
Marks a lambda parameter that is called from another execution context. Non-local returns are forbidden in it.
Lets public inline functions use an internal declaration. The declaration is public in the bytecode.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why the compiler made them write `crossinline` in `inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T) = withPrinter(Callable { block() })`. Explain, in your own words, what could go wrong without it and what they give up by adding it.
explain_back.answer: Because the function is inline, the caller's lambda is pasted into the caller, and normally a bare `return` in it would return from the caller. Here the lambda isn't called directly: it's called inside a `Callable` that the printer library runs, maybe later and maybe on another thread. By then the caller's function may already have returned, so a `return` from inside the `Callable` can't mean "return from the caller". The compiler can't allow that, so it asks for `crossinline`. With `crossinline`, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a `Callable` class it generates for that call site, and in exchange callers may not write a bare `return` in the block. They can still use a labeled return like `return@printing`. `noinline` would also compile, but it keeps the lambda as a separate object, which is the fix for storing a lambda, not for calling it somewhere else.
